accuracy.evidence: Eye-safety facts checked against the NHS (solar retinopathy: looking at the Sun can permanently damage the retina; never look at the Sun, even with sunglasses), the College of Optometrists and American Academy of Ophthalmology (choose sunglasses marked UV400, CE or BS EN ISO 12312-1; dark lenses without UV filters can dilate the pupil; a wide-brimmed hat reduces UV to the eyes), WHO Global Solar UV Index (fresh snow reflects up to 80% of UV; light cloud lets most UV through) and NASA eclipse safety guidance (pinhole projection, back to the Sun). Lux values follow the standard table: classroom or office 320-500, overcast day about 1,000, daylight in shade 10,000-25,000, direct sun up to about 100,000. Pinhole image width = distance × 0.0093 from the Sun's 0.53° angular size (1 m gives 9.3 mm). Parameterised answers a, 400*a and 2 are whole numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs documented in children's ideas about light and the Sun (Osborne et al., SPACE project report on light; NHS eclipse advice): sunglasses make it safe to look at the Sun (predict 1, card 3, p3, challenge 'glasses'), a quick look or a cloudy day is fine (gear tile 'A quick look', robot saying 1, m4, challenge 'quick' and 'cloud'), any dark glasses protect (gear tile 'Dark toy glasses', robot saying 3, m3, challenge 'dark'), the Sun is like a big lamp (predict 2 and the light meter's 250× bar, challenge 'bright'), and binoculars or telescopes help (card 5, robot saying 5, challenge 'bino').

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is about keeping eyes safe from sunlight: judge six illustrated ways of looking near the Sun, tap four places to fill light-meter bars in lux on one scale (the full-sun bar dwarfs the classroom), dress a child by tapping protective gear onto them (hat brim, UV400 glasses, shade canopy) while distractors are refused, and drag a pinhole viewer's screen along a cm rail so the Sun's picture grows to 3, 6 and 9 mm. flagsun (523) covers sunlight warming surfaces and flageye (1002) the parts of the eye; neither covers protection, brightness in lux or pinhole viewing. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_sunsafe.js under 30% similar to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds out by doing: each measured place adds its bar to one shared scale with 'about 50 times as bright as the classroom', so the size of the Sun's brightness is seen, not told; choosing toy glasses gets the reason dark lenses are not enough; in the pinhole scene the picture width updates in mm as the screen moves, and Check names whether to move closer or further and the distance that would work, so the child discovers that further away gives a bigger picture.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Can you look straight at the Sun if you wear sunglasses?' (yes) before the safe-or-not cards, 'How much brighter is full sun than a bright classroom?' (about twice) before the light meter, and 'To make the Sun's picture bigger, where should the screen go?' (closer) before the pinhole rail. The step completion message reveals the child's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions, each with two tagged wrong answers. why() has six distinct messages: glasses (sunglasses are for bright days, not for looking at the Sun), quick (even a quick look can hurt), dark (look for UV400 or CE), bright (100,000 against 400 lux, about 250 times), cloud (clouds move and light gets through) and bino (binoculars gather more light). Each names the slip and gives the safe action.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and plain words (bright, burn, brim, shade, bounce) and passes the family kid FK limit; the adult text names retina, UV, lux and the sunglasses marks and passes the adult limit. Canvas notes shrink to fit at 360 px, and light-meter labels sit in dark text on pale blue and amber bars so they stay readable.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one point: the Sun is far brighter than lamps (with the 250× figure), never look at it and why sunglasses and binoculars do not help, three ways to protect eyes, and reflections, clouds and pinhole viewing. The adult text gives the Year 3 requirement and key words, the medical facts with the marks to look for, three named mistakes, and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and under 12% overlap with every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in dark theme at rest and part-way through each Show me: the safe-or-not card fills 80% of the width with Safe and Not safe buttons 64 px tall, the four places sit in a 2 x 2 grid with the bars below, the gear tiles take 70% of the width beside the child, and the pinhole rail spans the canvas with a large marker and a 54 px Check key. Every canvas action has a button twin, including Closer and Further.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: Safe or Not safe (named with the card), each place to measure, each protective item, Closer, Further and Check, and Right or Slip. Each measurement, the picture width and every result are spoken through c.say and the canvas aria-label; challenge feedback is a polite live region. Safety is stated in words, never by colour alone. The walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
